- region "Sidebar":
  - article:
    - paragraph: A substantial fraction of the U.S. population lives in close proximity to traffic, and the number of vehicle-miles traveled has grown 40% from 1990 to 2010. Residential proximity to traffic has been associated with various health impacts, particularly asthma exacerbation and possibly onset of asthma, as well as mortality rates. Traffic proximity is also associated with noise, which is a risk factor for various health problems. Workplace and transportation-related noise have been associated with release of stress hormones; sleep disturbance; hypertension; altered heart rate; ischemic heart disease; myocardial infarction; and, among the elderly, risk of stroke. Whether noise or other factors account for it, local traffic volume is a predictor of stress (which itself is associated with significant health risks).
    - paragraph
    - paragraph:
      - text: Traffic proximity is given as a count of vehicles per day within 500 meters of a block centroid, divided by distance in meters, presented as the population-weighted average of blocks in each block group. Adjustments are made so that the minimum distance used is reasonable when very small. More information is available at
      - link "the mobile source pollution website":
        - /url: https://www.epa.gov/mobile-source-pollution
      - text: ". Source: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), 2019. EJSCREEN Technical Documentation."

- region "Sidebar":
  - article:
    - paragraph: Air toxics, often referred to as hazardous air pollutants (HAPs), are pollutants that are known or suspected to cause cancer or other serious health effects, such as reproductive effects or birth defects, or adverse environmental effects. The Environmental Protection Agency regulates 187 chemicals under its HAP program. Most air toxics originate from transportation and industry, including motor vehicles, industrial facilities and power plants.
    - paragraph: The National Air Toxics Assessment (NATA) calculates a hazard quotient, which is the ratio of ambient air concentration to a chemical’s health-based reference concentration (from the EPA’s Integrated Risk Information System). No adverse health effects are expected from exposure if the hazard quotient is less than one. A hazard index is the sum of hazard quotients for chemicals that cause adverse effects through the same toxic mechanism.
    - paragraph
    - paragraph: The hazard index for respiratory effects represents the cumulative impacts of all the relevant air toxics for which respiratory effects were the key health effect. More information is available at the air toxics website (https://www.epa.gov/haps), the NATA website (https://www.epa.gov/national-air-toxics-assessment).
    - paragraph
    - paragraph: "Source: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), 2019. EJSCREEN Technical Documentation."

- region "Sidebar":
  - article:
    - paragraph:
      - text: The EPA’s National Air Toxics Assessment (NATA) provides an estimate of lifetime inhalation cancer risk, aggregated as a cumulative risk for the combination of all analyzed hazardous air pollutants (HAPs). The air pollutants in the NATA include likely or known carcinogens such as formaldehyde, benzene, chloroprene, and coke oven emissions, as well as important sources of noncancer impact such as acrolein, DPM and chlorine. Hazardous air pollutants are emitted from a wide variety of sources and disperse around the sources, especially downwind. In some cases, these substances react with other constituents in the atmosphere or break down to other chemicals, and most are eventually removed through precipitation or other atmospheric processes. People are exposed in their daily activities in and around their homes, at school or work, and while moving about the area. They inhale the substances, exhale or excrete some portion of them, and have the potential for incurring adverse effects from the portion that stays in the body. More information is available at the
      - link "air toxics website":

- region "Sidebar":
  - article:
    - paragraph: The EPA's EJ Screen uses the most recent data from the National-Scale Air Toxics Assessment (NATA), which includes estimates of diesel particulate matter concentration in the air (measured in micrograms per cubic meter). NATA uses emissions estimates from the National Emissions Inventory (NEI), which is updated every three years. The NEI includes all of the Toxics Release Inventory (TRI) reporting facilities that release hazardous air pollutants, along with many other sources of air pollutants, such as motor vehicles. EPA’s NATA website has extensive documentation of all of the data and methods used in developing the NATA indicators, as well as discussions of uncertainty, caveats, and limitations in the NATA estimates. That information is not repeated here, but it is important that anyone using NATA data understand these issues, so anyone using EJSCREEN should consult the NATA documentation (https://www.epa.gov/national-air-toxics-assessment).

- region "Sidebar":
  - article:
    - paragraph: PM2.5 is particulate matter that is 2.5 microns or less in diameter. Measured as an annual average concentration in micrograms per cubic meter. Common sources of PM2.5 emissions include power plants and industrial facilities. Secondary PM2.5 can form from gases, such as oxides of nitrogen (NOx) or sulfur dioxide (SO2), reacting in the atmosphere. EPA’s work associated with the PM National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) has documented the health effects associated with exposure to PM2.5, including elevated risk of premature mortality from cardiovascular diseases or lung cancer, and increased health problems such as asthma attacks. Certain demographic groups, such as those with lower educational attainment, children, the elderly and those with low socio-economic status, appear to be more susceptible to a given exposure to particulate matter. More information is available at the PM2.5 website (https://www.epa.gov/pm-pollution).
    - paragraph
    - paragraph: "Source: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), 2019. EJSCREEN Technical Documentation."

- region "Sidebar":
  - article:
    - paragraph: Ozone (O3) is not usually emitted directly into the air, but is created at ground level by a chemical reaction between oxides of nitrogen (NOx) and volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in the presence of sunlight. These ozone precursors are emitted by motor vehicles, industrial facilities and power plants as well as natural sources. Ground-level ozone is the primary constituent of "smog." Toxicological and epidemiological studies have established an association between exposure to ambient ozone and a variety of health outcomes, including reduction in lung function, increased inflammation and increased hospital admissions and mortality. Several subpopulations may experience susceptibility to ozone-induced health effects. These subpopulations include older adults, children, individuals with preexisting pulmonary disease and those with higher exposure levels such as outdoor workers.
    - paragraph
    - paragraph: More information is available at the ground-level ozone website (https://www.epa.gov/ground-level-ozone-pollution).
    - paragraph

    - paragraph: "Source: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), 2019. EJSCREEN Technical Documentation."
